# 2006 Xterra Doesn't Always Start

A vehicle that cranks but fails to catch on the first attempt, then starts reliably after a pause and a second try, is almost always an ignition system or fuel delivery issue rather than a battery problem. Since you've already confirmed the battery is fresh and replaced without changing the behavior, we can rule out low voltage as the primary culprit. The fact that the engine runs perfectly once it is started further isolates the fault to the moment of startup: either the spark isn't occurring consistently at TDC, or the fuel system isn't building sufficient pressure instantly.

The most common cause for this specific symptom in a 2006 Nissan Xterra is a failing ignition coil pack or a weak crankshaft position sensor. The engine control module (ECM) relies on the crankshaft position sensor to tell it exactly when to fire the coils and inject fuel. If that sensor signal is weak or intermittent, the ECM might skip the first cycle but successfully fire on the next attempt once the RPM rises slightly or the thermal characteristics of the component shift. This explains why there are no check engine lights; the system often detects a misfire only after it has occurred, and by the time you wait 20 seconds with the key out, the issue resolves itself before the car enters limp mode or stores a persistent fault code.

Another frequent culprit in this era of Nissan is the fuel pump relay located under the dashboard on the driver's side. These relays are known to develop internal resistance that causes them to chatter or fail to close fully during the initial power request from the ECM. When you turn the key, the pump may not prime immediately. Waiting 20 seconds allows the residual pressure in the lines to stabilize or gives the relay a chance to reset, which is why the second attempt works instantly. To diagnose this without disassembling the engine bay yet, listen closely to the fuel pump. You should hear a distinct whirring sound for about two seconds when you first turn the key to the "On" position before cranking. If that sound is missing or sounds faint, the relay or the pump itself is suspect.

Before tearing into the ignition coil pack, which costs significantly more than a relay, verify the fuel pressure. Connect a gauge to the test port on the fuel rail and watch the needle as soon as you turn the key to "On." It should jump up to approximately 40-50 PSI within half a second. If the gauge stays at zero or climbs very slowly, the issue is isolated to the pump or the relay. If pressure builds normally but the car still won't start on the first crank, the ignition coil pack is the likely failure point. The secondary coils in the Xterra's pack are notorious for developing micro-fractures that cause a loss of spark under high load or cold conditions.

You can also check the main power supply to these components. A corroded ground strap between the engine block and the chassis can introduce enough resistance to mimic an intermittent failure, especially as the metal expands and contracts with temperature changes. Inspect the negative battery terminal and the engine ground points for white oxidation or loose bolts. Tightening a single ground connection often resolves "noisy" electrical behavior that mimics sensor failures.

If you have access to a scan tool capable of live data logging, record the crankshaft position sensor signal while attempting to start. A dropping voltage reading on that line during the cranking attempt would confirm the sensor is dying. However, given the low cost and high failure rate of the fuel pump relay on this platform, swapping it for a known good unit is often the most efficient first step before moving to more invasive diagnostics like replacing the coil pack or sensors.
